title: Epsilon Indi B
blurb: Two brown dwarfs 12 light-years away, sliding 4.7″ a year.
story: Epsilon Indi B is a pair of brown dwarfs — too small to shine like stars — circling the star Epsilon Indi, only 12 light-years from us. Because they are so close, they slide across the sky by about 4.7 arcseconds every year. Blink the first and the last visit: the dot in the middle steps toward the south-east while the stars around it stay put.

spectrum.hint: The measurements scatter too much to read a pattern. That happens when an object is so bright that it overloads the detector, or when it is changing while SPHEREx watches. Each point is a separate exposure, taken at a different time.

doodles.explain: This one is always there but slides steadily toward the south-east: 6.6 arcseconds (1.1 SPHEREx pixels) in 17 months, about 4.6 arcseconds a year. Steady drift like this is how a nearby star or brown dwarf looks from Earth. (Something this close also wobbles with the seasons, by up to an arcsecond: over a year or so that wobble is part of the number.) This is * eps Ind B, a known brown dwarf (SIMBAD). The catalogue lists 4.68 arcseconds a year; these images give 4.6 ± 0.4.

source: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (collections spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3)
